content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, the dog is a predominantly negative symbol of uncleanness, contempt, and moral impurity. It represents those outside the covenant community or hostile to what is holy: the profane, the wicked, unbelievers, and (in the Gospels) Gentiles as viewed from a Jewish covenantal perspective. By extension it commonly symbolizes false teachers and apostates who return to their sin.","primary_basis":["Matthew 7:6 (do not give what is holy to dogs)","Matthew 15:26-27 / Mark 7:27-28 (children's bread thrown to the dogs, in the Canaanite/Syrophoenician woman episode)","Philippians 3:2 (beware of the dogs, of evil workers)","Revelation 22:15 (outside are the dogs, sorcerers, immoral persons)","2 Peter 2:22 quoting Proverbs 26:11 (the dog returns to its own vomit)","Deuteronomy 23:18 (the wages of a dog not brought into the LORD's house)","Psalm 22:16,20 (dogs surround me, evildoers encircle)","1 Samuel 24:14 and 2 Samuel 9:8 ('dead dog' as expression of worthlessness and self-abasement)","Isaiah 56:10-11 (blind watchmen as mute, greedy dogs)","1 Kings 21:19-24; 2 Kings 9:36 (dogs licking blood/eating Jezebel as sign of disgrace and judgment)"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Dogs as a specific figure for Gentiles or the nations outside Israel's covenant, especially in exegesis of Matthew 15 / Mark 7; some interpreters soften this by noting the diminutive 'little dogs/house dogs' and read the exchange as opening blessing to Gentiles.","basis":["Matthew 15:21-28","Mark 7:24-30"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Dogs as false teachers, Judaizers, or heretics who threaten the church — an inversion by Paul of the Jewish epithet against Gentiles.","basis":["Philippians 3:2","Isaiah 56:10-11","2 Peter 2:22"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Dogs as apostates or backsliders who return to former sin after professing conversion.","basis":["2 Peter 2:20-22","Proverbs 26:11"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"'Dog' in Deuteronomy 23:18 read as a technical term for a male cult prostitute rather than a literal animal or general slur — a reading held in scholarly and some translation traditions.","basis":["Deuteronomy 23:17-18"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"'Dogs' in Revelation 22:15 read specifically as the sexually immoral or perverse (linked to Deut 23:18) rather than a general term for the wicked.","basis":["Revelation 22:15","Deuteronomy 23:18"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"A positive symbolism of loyalty, watchfulness, and faithfulness — largely extra-biblical or paracanonical (Tobit's dog; medieval iconography; the Dominican 'Domini canes' pun on hounds of the Lord; the Syrophoenician woman's humble acceptance of the term as a model of persistent faith).","basis":["Tobit 6:2; 11:4 (deuterocanonical)","Matthew 15:27-28 (the woman's response commended)","Later Christian iconographic and homiletic tradition rather than direct biblical texts"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Dogs as instruments or images of divine judgment and disgrace (scavenging corpses, licking blood).","basis":["1 Kings 14:11; 16:4; 21:19-24","2 Kings 9:10,36","Jeremiah 15:3","Psalm 68:23"],"prominence":"common"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is a well-recognized, broadly settled consensus that biblical dog imagery is overwhelmingly negative: in the ancient Near Eastern context dogs were semi-wild scavengers, not household pets, so the term functions as a slur denoting uncleanness, contempt, and exclusion from the holy. The main interpretive debates concern application (whom the dogs represent in a given passage — Gentiles, false teachers, apostates, the sexually immoral, or the wicked generally) rather than the basic valence. Positive dog symbolism (loyalty, fidelity) is essentially a later Christian and deuterocanonical development, not the dominant biblical sense."}
